raw_case_text:
A 57-year-old banker presented with high-grade fever for 6 weeks and severe backache for 4 weeks. He went on frequent official trips to different cities and had history of consuming foods in restaurants on these trips. He denied history of diarrhoea, joint pain, weight loss, bowel/bladder incontinence, urinary retention and motor weakness. He was a known case of systemic hypertension for 17 years and diabetes mellitus for 1 month and was on regular medicines.
Examination of the spine revealed lower thoracic tenderness and restricted lateral flexion. He had Class I obesity (body mass index 33). Blood investigations showed high erythrocyte sedimentation rate and mildly elevated C-reactive protein levels [Table 1].
In this patient with subacute history of back pain and fever, we considered differential diagnoses of infective spondylodiscitis, epidural and paraspinal abscess. Magnetic resonance imaging showed contrast enhancement in the 11th and 12th thoracic vertebra and intervening disc [Figure 1].
Computed tomography-guided biopsy from thoracic vertebra showed necrotic bone with lymphocyte and neutrophil infiltration. Biopsy specimen and blood culture showed growth of NARST. Widal test was positive for Salmonella paratyphi A in 1280 dilutions. Drug susceptibility testing showed sensitivity to chloramphenicol, ceftriaxone, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and azithromycin. Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) for ciprofloxacin and azithromycin were 0.5 mug/dL and 8 mug/dL, respectively. We started injection azithromycin 1 g intravenously once daily. However, he continued to have high-grade fever 1 week after initiation of azithromycin. Reasons for persistent fever that we thought of were metastatic and endovascular foci of infection and suboptimal antibiotic delivery due to poor bone penetration. Echocardiogram, ultrasound abdomen and bone scan were normal. In view of clinical failure with azithromycin, we decided to start intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g once daily) and oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (800/160 mg) twice daily. Defervescence occurred 5 days after initiation of ceftriaxone. He was seen by spine surgeons who advised conservative management. He was managed with intravenous azithromycin and ceftriaxone for 2 weeks followed by oral azithromycin (1 g once daily), ciprofloxacin (750 mg twice daily) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 10 weeks. At his 3-month follow-up, back pain had decreased by 90%. Repeat MRI spine showed disease regression.1

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old male banker presented with a 6-week history of high-grade fever and a 4-week history of severe thoracic back pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed persistent high-grade fever for 6 weeks joined 2 weeks later by severe lower thoracic backache.
subjective.past_medical_history: 17-year history of systemic hypertension and 1-month history of diabetes mellitus on regular medications; Class I obesity (BMI 33 kg/m^2). Occupation: banker with frequent business travel to various cities and regular consumption of restaurant food.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 6-week high-grade fever and 4-week severe back pain. Pertinent negatives: no diarrhea, peripheral joint pain, weight loss, bowel or bladder incontinence, urinary retention, or lower limb motor weakness.

objective.physical_examination: BMI was 33 kg/m^2 (Class I obesity). Spinal examination demonstrated localized lower thoracic vertebral tenderness and restricted lateral spinal flexion, with intact motor and sphincter function.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood tests showed elevated ESR and mildly elevated CRP. Widal test was strongly positive for Salmonella paratyphi A at a 1:1,280 dilution. Transthoracic echocardiogram, abdominal ultrasound, and technetium bone scan were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic spine MRI revealed T11-T12 spondylodiscitis with contrast enhancement of the T11 and T12 vertebral bodies and intervening intervertebral disc. CT-guided biopsy of the thoracic vertebra demonstrated necrotic bone with lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltration. Both the vertebral biopsy culture and blood culture grew nalidixic acid-resistant Salmonella Typhi (NARST), susceptible to chloramphenicol, ceftriaxone, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and azithromycin, with a ciprofloxacin MIC of 0.5 µg/dL and an azithromycin MIC of 8 µg/dL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Thoracic infective spondylodiscitis (T11-T12) caused by nalidixic acid-resistant Salmonella Typhi (NARST), confirmed by both CT-guided vertebral bone biopsy culture and blood culture along with spine MRI and bone histopathology. Endocarditis was excluded via echocardiography. Initial monotherapy with intravenous azithromycin (1 g once daily) failed to resolve high-grade fever after 1 week due to poor bone penetration. Adding intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g once daily) and oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (800/160 mg twice daily) produced defervescence within 5 days. Under conservative non-operative spine management, he completed 2 weeks of IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin followed by 10 weeks of oral combination therapy (azithromycin 1 g once daily, ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 800/160 mg twice daily); at 3-month follow-up, back pain had decreased by 90% and repeat spine MRI confirmed regression of spondylodiscitis.
